title: Renal & Liver Chemistry Fundamentals

references.label: Standard clinical chemistry laboratory textbooks/manuals (e.g. Tietz Fundamentals of Clinical Chemistry)
CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

summary: Renal function panels and liver function panels are two of the most common clinical chemistry groupings, each combining several analytes whose pattern — not any single value — provides the clinically useful picture.
explanation: A typical renal panel includes analytes such as blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine, interpreted alongside electrolytes; both BUN and creatinine rise as glomerular filtration falls, but each is also affected by non-renal factors (e.g. BUN by protein intake/hydration, creatinine by muscle mass), which is why they are interpreted together and trended over time rather than as an isolated single value. A typical liver panel includes enzymes that leak from damaged hepatocytes (e.g. ALT, AST — measured using the kinetic enzyme-assay principle already covered generically), markers of cholestasis/biliary obstruction (e.g. alkaline phosphatase, GGT), and markers of synthetic/excretory function (e.g. albumin, bilirubin). The overall pattern across these analytes — not any one number — points toward a hepatocellular, cholestatic, or mixed process, and definitive diagnosis and any treatment decision remain a clinical, not laboratory-alone, judgment.

comparison.right: Reflects filtration/excretory function, affected by non-renal factors too
Pattern across markers, not one value, suggests process type

commonMisconceptions: Treating a single elevated liver enzyme as diagnostic of a specific disease — enzyme elevation patterns are non-specific and are interpreted as a panel, in clinical context.
